title: One library, several builds
cards/0/body: A project can build for several targets at once. You get several DLLs, and NuGet packs each one into its own folder in the package.
cards/1/body: Each consuming project takes the nearest compatible build. Given net8.0 and netstandard2.0, a .NET 10 app takes net8.0: it is closer and uses more features. Revit 2024 takes netstandard2.0.
cards/2/task: Revit 2025 should get a net8.0 build with the new APIs, while Revit 2024 and Unity keep working. Two targets at most.
cards/3/q: Targets are net8.0 and netstandard2.0. Which build does a .NET 10 app take?
cards/3/explain: net8.0 is compatible with .NET 10 and closer to it than the standard.
cards/4/body: Where APIs differ, preprocessor symbols help. The SDK defines them for each target automatically.
cards/4/code:
#if NET8_0_OR_GREATER
    var hash = SHA256.HashData(bytes);           // new API
#else
    using var sha = SHA256.Create();
    var hash = sha.ComputeHash(bytes);           // works everywhere
#endif
cards/5/q: Code only for the .NET Framework build
cards/5/explain: NETFRAMEWORK is defined for net48 and other Framework targets.
cards/6/task: A plugin with separate code for Revit 2024 (net48) and Revit 2025 (net8.0), plus a shared part that must work in Unity.
cards/7/body: A plugin for several Revit versions is usually one project with the targets net48 and net8.0-windows (the -windows suffix is needed for WPF). References to RevitAPI.dll are added conditionally, with the right version for each target.
cards/8/q: Match each symbol to when it is defined
cards/9/q: Why bother with several targets if netstandard2.0 works everywhere?
cards/9/options/0: To use newer, faster APIs on new platforms without losing the old ones
cards/9/explain: The standard itself is not slow. It just lacks the APIs that came later.
